endorsements.title: CHAI AI governance frameworks (playbooks)
endorsements.quote: Defining escalation triggers in advance prevents both under-reporting (monitors unsure what rises to that level) and over-reporting (every minor anomaly flooding the committee).

endorsements.title: Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework: Generative AI Profile (NIST AI 600-1)
endorsements.issuer: National Institute of Standards and Technology
endorsements.quote: Establish and regularly review specific criteria that warrants the deactivation of GAI systems in accordance with set risk tolerances and appetites.

endorsements.title: CHAI Responsible AI Guide (Assurance Standards Guide)
endorsements.quote: Finally the team should consider whether thresholds for data quality have been established (i.e., the extent to which the AI solution will continue to be safe and operate if there is a defect noted in data quality).

endorsements.title: Responsible artificial intelligence integration framework for psychiatric guidelines
endorsements.quote: Escalation protocols for ethically sensitive or high-risk outputs, preventing automated propagation of potentially harmful recommendations.

endorsements.title: Artificial intelligence in traumatic stress treatment: The TRUST framework for ethical development, clinical applications, and research advancement
endorsements.quote: During deployment, crisis escalation protocols with defined response times must be implemented and actively monitored, “human-in-the-loop” oversight for high-risk situations must be maintained, real-time safety monitoring interfaces should be used, and defined check-ins with clinicians engaging with the AI tool should be prioritized.

endorsements.title: Ethical Considerations in Personal Health Large Language Models
endorsements.quote: As a conceptual response framework, critical adverse events trigger graduated action according to scope and severity, ranging from session-level termination of an affected thread to feature-level disabling of implicated functionality or, when risk is systemic, global suspension of the application.

commentary.bottom_line: Six sources, three frameworks and three commentaries, recommend that health systems set and periodically revisit predefined triggers for escalating, re-reviewing, suspending, or deactivating AI tools, but no supplied study tests whether doing so leads to faster or more reliable action on degraded performance. The recommendation currently rests on expert consensus and conceptual reasoning.

perspectives.view: No study in the supplied set tests predefined thresholds or triggers, and no study documents the hazard of unacted-upon degradation. All six endorsements are frameworks or commentaries. Under GRADE conventions, this leaves no body of evidence to rate. The agreement across sources reflects shared expert judgment, which should not be read as evidence of effect.

The endorsing sources describe graduated responses, ranging from ending a single session to suspending an entire application, and they tie those responses to the scope and severity of an event. This logic mirrors other safety escalation schemes. No supplied study shows whether predefined triggers catch degradation before it reaches patients, or which threshold levels balance missed signals against alert overload.

NIST AI 600-1 asks organizations to set and review deactivation criteria tied to their stated risk tolerances. The CHAI guides frame thresholds as part of assurance and governance practice. These documents are voluntary guidance. In the supplied material they do not create a binding requirement, and they leave the specific threshold values to each organization.

commentary.research_gap: Studies are needed that compare deployments with and without predefined escalation and deactivation thresholds. Useful outcomes would include time from detected performance drift to governance action, the number of harmful outputs reaching patients, and the volume of reviews committees receive. Separate work should examine how threshold levels are chosen and whether scheduled review of those thresholds changes decisions.
commentary.underserved_note: No supplied study tested this practice in any population, so no evidence covers Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy patients. Because performance degradation can differ across subgroups, thresholds set only on aggregate metrics may fail to trigger when a tool degrades for these groups. No supplied study has examined this question.
